Omani abalone, Haliotis mariae, attains a maximum shell length of 13.5 centimetres [Li = 13.5 centimetres], making it one of the larger abalone species in the Arabian Sea. Field surveys along the Dhofar coastline have repeatedly confirmed this asymptotic dimension, which is comparable to the maximum lengths reported for the closely related Haliotis rubra but somewhat smaller than the largest individuals of Haliotis tuberculata. Females undergo a significant developmental milestone when they reach a shell width of 6.5 centimetres at puberty [Lp = 6.5 centimetres at puberty], a measurement derived from the relative length relationship observed in Haliotis rubra. This transition marks the onset of reproductive competence and is a critical parameter for fishery management, as it helps define the minimum legal capture size necessary to protect spawning stock biomass. The pronounced allometric growth of the shell during the pre-pubertal phase shifts noticeably after maturity, with energy being increasingly directed toward gonadal development rather than somatic expansion.

Reproductive output in Haliotis mariae is remarkably high when maintained under optimal thermal conditions. At a sustained water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the maximum reproductive rate reaches approximately 2.3 million eggs per year [Ri = approximately 2.3 million eggs per year], a figure that reflects the prodigious fecundity typical of broadcast-spawning gastropods. This value was estimated by scaling the specific maximum reproductive rate reported for Haliotis rubra to the smaller body size of Omani abalone. The daily spawning events are tightly coupled with environmental cues such as lunar phase and phytoplankton blooms, ensuring that gamete synchrony is maximized during the breeding season. Field observations suggest that individual females can sustain this elevated output for several consecutive weeks, although the energetic cost of such high fecundity likely contributes to the relatively short reproductive lifespan observed in natural populations. The eggs themselves are minute, with each fertilised ovum measuring only about 0.02 millimetres in diameter.

From these tiny eggs emerges a larval stage characterised by minimal maternal provisioning. The wet weight at birth, corresponding to the late trochophore or early veliger stage, is approximately 0.0000042 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0000042 grams], a value derived from the spherical volume formula assuming the egg diameter of 0.02 millimetres. This exceptionally low initial mass imposes a stringent energetic bottleneck on the free-swimming larva, which must rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves until the onset of planktotrophic feeding. Once the veliger begins filtering phytoplankton from the water column, growth accelerates rapidly, and the prodissoconch shell expands appreciably within the first few days. The transition to the pediveliger stage, marked by the development of a foot and the ability to explore benthic substrates, occurs after roughly two to three weeks in the plankton. Settlement onto crustose coralline algae triggers the final metamorphic transformation into a post-larval juvenile.

Adults of Haliotis mariae exhibit a substantial somatic mass once the shell is excluded from the measurement. The shell-free wet weight of a large, reproductively active individual is approximately 132.7 grams [Wwi = approximately 132.7 grams], a figure based on the allometric relationship established for Haliotis tuberculata, which yields a total body mass of 1.3 kilograms at a shell length of 20 centimetres. Scaling this relationship down to the 13.5 centimetre maximum length of Omani abalone provides a reasonable estimate of tissue biomass available for commercial harvest. This soft-tissue mass consists predominantly of the large adductor muscle and the gonadal tissues, both of which fluctuate seasonally in accordance with the reproductive cycle. During the peak spawning period, the gonad may constitute nearly a third of the total visceral mass, reflecting the high gametic investment described earlier. Post-spawning, the adductor muscle becomes glycogen-depleted, and individuals enter a brief period of physiological recovery before the next reproductive bout.

Longevity data for Haliotis mariae, gathered from mark-recapture studies in the wild, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 7300 days [am = approximately 7300 days] under natural conditions sustained at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This value is somewhat shorter than the lifespan recorded for temperate abalone species such as Haliotis discus hannai but still considerable for a tropical marine gastropod. The temperature regime is crucial, as metabolic rates scale directly with thermal conditions; at persistently elevated temperatures, the accumulation of cellular damage accelerates, truncating the ultimate achievable age. Senescence in older individuals manifests as a gradual decline in gonadal output, a slowing of foot locomotion, and increased susceptibility to shell-boring parasites. The demographic structure of wild populations is heavily skewed toward younger age classes, primarily due to intense fishing pressure on larger, older individuals. Conservation efforts therefore focus on establishing marine protected areas where natural mortality can proceed undisturbed, allowing the full life cycle to be expressed.
